claim: Multiple embryonic origins give rise to forebrain oligodendrocytes (OLs).
source: Multiple embryonic origins give rise to forebrain oligodendrocytes (OLs), yet controversies and uncertainty exist regarding their differential contributions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Controversies and uncertainty exist regarding the differential contributions of multiple embryonic origins to forebrain oligodendrocytes.
source: Multiple embryonic origins give rise to forebrain oligodendrocytes (OLs), yet controversies and uncertainty exist regarding their differential contributions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as context for the study.

claim: LGE/CGE-derived OLs make minimum contributions to the neocortex.
source: We found that, contrary to the canonical view, LGE/CGE-derived OLs make minimum contributions to the neocortex and corpus callosum, but dominate piriform cortex and anterior commissure.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative data in the results section.

claim: LGE/CGE-derived OLs make minimum contributions to the corpus callosum.
source: We found that, contrary to the canonical view, LGE/CGE-derived OLs make minimum contributions to the neocortex and corpus callosum, but dominate piriform cortex and anterior commissure.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative data in the results section.

claim: LGE/CGE-derived OLs dominate piriform cortex.
source: We found that, contrary to the canonical view, LGE/CGE-derived OLs make minimum contributions to the neocortex and corpus callosum, but dominate piriform cortex and anterior commissure.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative data in the results section.

claim: LGE/CGE-derived OLs dominate anterior commissure.
source: We found that, contrary to the canonical view, LGE/CGE-derived OLs make minimum contributions to the neocortex and corpus callosum, but dominate piriform cortex and anterior commissure.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative data in the results section.

claim: MGE/POA-derived OLs are not entirely eliminated postnatally.
source: Additionally, MGE/POA-derived OLs, instead of being entirely eliminated, make small but sustained contribution to cortex with a distribution pattern distinctive from those derived from the dorsal origin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data showing MPOLs in adult mice.

claim: MGE/POA-derived OLs make small but sustained contribution to cortex.
source: Additionally, MGE/POA-derived OLs, instead of being entirely eliminated, make small but sustained contribution to cortex with a distribution pattern distinctive from those derived from the dorsal origin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative data in the results section.

claim: MGE/POA-derived OLs have a distribution pattern distinctive from those derived from the dorsal origin.
source: Additionally, MGE/POA-derived OLs, instead of being entirely eliminated, make small but sustained contribution to cortex with a distribution pattern distinctive from those derived from the dorsal origin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data showing spatial distribution patterns.

claim: Forebrain OLs arise from multiple embryonic origins.
source: Forebrain OLs arise from multiple embryonic origins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Previous fate-mapping study using Nkx2.1Cre reported consecutive and competing waves of OLs derived from medial ganglionic eminence/preoptic area (MGE/POA).
source: Previous fate-mapping study using Nkx2.1Cre (Xu et al., 2008), Gsh2Cre (Kessaris et al., 2006), and Emx1Cre (Gorski et al., 2002) reported consecutive and competing waves of OLs derived from medial ganglionic eminence/preoptic area (MGE/POA), lateral/caudal ganglionic eminences (LGE/CGE), and dorsal pallium (Kessaris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous fate-mapping study using Gsh2Cre reported consecutive and competing waves of OLs derived from lateral/caudal ganglionic eminences (LGE/CGE).
source: Previous fate-mapping study using Nkx2.1Cre (Xu et al., 2008), Gsh2Cre (Kessaris et al., 2006), and Emx1Cre (Gorski et al., 2002) reported consecutive and competing waves of OLs derived from medial ganglionic eminence/preoptic area (MGE/POA), lateral/caudal ganglionic eminences (LGE/CGE), and dorsal pallium (Kessaris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous fate-mapping study using Emx1Cre reported consecutive and competing waves of OLs derived from dorsal pallium.
source: Previous fate-mapping study using Nkx2.1Cre (Xu et al., 2008), Gsh2Cre (Kessaris et al., 2006), and Emx1Cre (Gorski et al., 2002) reported consecutive and competing waves of OLs derived from medial ganglionic eminence/preoptic area (MGE/POA), lateral/caudal ganglionic eminences (LGE/CGE), and dorsal pallium (Kessaris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The first wave of OLs generated by MGE/POA (MPOLs) was believed to be eliminated postnatally.
source: The first wave of OLs generated by MGE/POA (MPOLs) was believed to be eliminated postnatally, while those from the second and third waves (LCOLs and dOLs) survive and populate the cortex and corpus callosum at comparable proportions.
evidence: This is stated as the previous canonical view in the introduction.

claim: OLs from the second and third waves (LCOLs and dOLs) survive and populate the cortex and corpus callosum at comparable proportions according to the canonical model.
source: The first wave of OLs generated by MGE/POA (MPOLs) was believed to be eliminated postnatally, while those from the second and third waves (LCOLs and dOLs) survive and populate the cortex and corpus callosum at comparable proportions.
evidence: This is stated as the previous canonical view in the introduction.

claim: Several studies provided both supporting and contradicting evidence to the canonical model of forebrain OL origins.
source: Several other studies provided both supporting and contradicting evidence to this model (Nakahira et al., 2006; Tsoa et al., 2014; Naruse et al., 2016; Orduz et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2021; Tripathi et al., 2011; Winkler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Gsh2 was recently found to be expressed in dorsal progenitors.
source: Moreover, Gsh2 was recently found to be expressed in dorsal progenitors (Zhang et al., 2020), casting doubt on the interpretation of lineage tracing data from Gsh2Cre.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: The expression of Gsh2 in dorsal progenitors casts doubt on the interpretation of lineage tracing data from Gsh2Cre.
source: Moreover, Gsh2 was recently found to be expressed in dorsal progenitors (Zhang et al., 2020), casting doubt on the interpretation of lineage tracing data from Gsh2Cre.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited finding about Gsh2 expression.

claim: Neocortical OLs are primarily composed of dOLs, rather than similar proportions of LCOLs and dOLs.
source: We found that neocortical OLs are primarily composed of dOLs, rather than similar proportions of LCOLs and dOLs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by quantitative data in the results section.

claim: LCOLs and dOLs made comparable contributions to piriform cortex.
source: In contrast, LCOLs and dOLs made comparable contributions to piriform cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by quantitative data in the results section.

claim: MPOLs persist in the cortex beyond adulthood with a unique spatial pattern distinct from that of the dOLs.
source: We also found that although MPOLs only make a small contribution, they do persist in the cortex beyond adulthood with a unique spatial pattern distinct from that of the dOLs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data showing MPOLs in 1-year-old mice.

claim: dOLs are the vast majority in corpus callosum.
source: In the two major white matter commissure tracts, dOLs are the vast majority in corpus callosum but make little contribution to anterior commissure, while LCOLs behaved the opposite.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by quantitative data in the results section.

claim: dOLs make little contribution to anterior commissure.
source: In the two major white matter commissure tracts, dOLs are the vast majority in corpus callosum but make little contribution to anterior commissure, while LCOLs behaved the opposite.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by quantitative data in the results section.

claim: LCOLs make little contribution to corpus callosum but dominate anterior commissure.
source: In the two major white matter commissure tracts, dOLs are the vast majority in corpus callosum but make little contribution to anterior commissure, while LCOLs behaved the opposite.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by quantitative data in the results section.

claim: Opalin encodes oligodendrocytic myelin paranodal and inner loop protein that are specifically expressed in differentiated OLs.
source: Opalin (also known as Tmem10) encodes oligodendrocytic myelin paranodal and inner loop protein that are specifically expressed in differentiated OLs (Kippert et al., 2008; Yoshikawa et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2013; Marques et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Flp-mediated recombination by OpalinFlp enables highly specific, efficient, and irreversible OL labeling.
source: Flp-mediated recombination by this driver (hereinafter referred to as OpalinFlp for simplicity) enables highly specific, efficient, and irreversible OL labeling, while the tTA2 component offers the flexibility for OL-specific labeling in tunable densities (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D-F demonstrating specificity and efficiency.

claim: The tTA2 component of OpalinP2A-Flpo-T2A-tTA2 offers the flexibility for OL-specific labeling in tunable densities.
source: Flp-mediated recombination by this driver (hereinafter referred to as OpalinFlp for simplicity) enables highly specific, efficient, and irreversible OL labeling, while the tTA2 component offers the flexibility for OL-specific labeling in tunable densities (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D-F demonstrating variable regional density.

claim: Both Flp and tTA2 reporting systems are highly specific, as shown by the complete co-localization of fluorescent protein (XFP) with OL marker (CC1) and lack of co-staining with neuronal marker (NeuN) or astrocyte marker (Sox9).
source: Both reporting systems are highly specific, as shown by the complete co-localization of fluorescent protein (XFP) with OL marker (CC1) and lack of co-staining with neuronal marker (NeuN) or astrocyte marker (Sox9).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Close to complete OL labeling was achieved by Flp-dependent H2B-GFP reporter in all analyzed regions.
source: Close to complete OL labeling was achieved by Flp-dependent H2B-GFP reporter in all analyzed regions (green dots), while sparser labeling with variable regional density was achieved by tTA2-dependent tdTomato reporter driven by TRE promoter (red dots).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Sparser labeling with variable regional density was achieved by tTA2-dependent tdTomato reporter driven by TRE promoter.
source: Close to complete OL labeling was achieved by Flp-dependent H2B-GFP reporter in all analyzed regions (green dots), while sparser labeling with variable regional density was achieved by tTA2-dependent tdTomato reporter driven by TRE promoter (red dots).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The vast majority of neocortical OLs were dOLs but not LCOLs.
source: The first major deviation is that, instead of comparable contributions by dOLs and LCOLs, the vast majority of neocortical OLs were dOLs but not LCOLs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by density and ASPA ratio data in Figure 2.

claim: The densities and ASPA ratios of dOLs are much higher than those of LCOLs in the neocortex.
source: The densities (Figure 2G–I and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–F) and ASPA ratios (Figure 2J) of dOLs are much higher than those of LCOLs.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2G-J and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-F.

claim: The genuine contribution of LCOLs to the neocortex could be even lesser than the current observation due to incomplete recombination in combinatorial reporters and relatively low Cre activity in the dorsal MGE of Nkx2.1Cre.
source: Considering the possibility of incomplete recombination in combinatorial reporters, and the relatively low Cre activity in the dorsal MGE of Nkx2.1Cre (Xu et al., 2008), the genuine contribution of LCOLs to the neocortex could be even lesser than our current observation.
evidence: This is an inference based on technical considerations and cited literature.

claim: The large quantity of neocortical OLs labeled by Gsh2Cre in previous study most likely were predominantly dOLs generated by Gsh2+ dorsal progenitors, rather than bona fide LCOLs.
source: Therefore, the large quantity of neocortical OLs labeled by Gsh2Cre in previous study (Kessaris et al., 2006) or by GFP in OpalinFlp::Gsh2Cre::RC::FLTG (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) most likely were predominantly dOLs generated by Gsh2+ dorsal progenitors (Zhang et al., 2020), rather than bona fide LCOLs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and cited literature about Gsh2 expression in dorsal progenitors.

claim: Cortical MPOLs are not completely depleted postnatally.
source: The second major deviation is that cortical MPOLs are not completely depleted postnatally.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data showing MPOLs in adult mice.

claim: MPOLs make a small but continued contribution with a unique spatial distribution pattern.
source: Instead, they make a small but continued contribution with a unique spatial distribution pattern (Figure 2I, J and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative data in Figure 2I, J and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–G.

claim: MPOLs display a clear rostrocaudal density decline.
source: MPOLs display a clear rostrocaudal density decline (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F), a higher density in somatosensory cortex (SS) than motor cortex (Mo) (Figure 2I), and a laminar preference toward layer 4 (L4) in SS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F.

claim: MPOLs have a higher density in somatosensory cortex (SS) than motor cortex (Mo).
source: MPOLs display a clear rostrocaudal density decline (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F), a higher density in somatosensory cortex (SS) than motor cortex (Mo) (Figure 2I), and a laminar preference toward layer 4 (L4) in SS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: MPOLs have a laminar preference toward layer 4 (L4) in SS.
source: MPOLs display a clear rostrocaudal density decline (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F), a higher density in somatosensory cortex (SS) than motor cortex (Mo) (Figure 2I), and a laminar preference toward layer 4 (L4) in SS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: The distribution of dOLs and LCOLs do not vary significantly across the rostrocaudal axis.
source: In contrast, the distribution of dOLs and LCOLs do not vary significantly across the rostrocaudal axis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F) or between Mo and SS (Figure 2G, H), but exhibits increased density toward deeper layers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F.

claim: The distribution of dOLs and LCOLs do not vary significantly between Mo and SS.
source: In contrast, the distribution of dOLs and LCOLs do not vary significantly across the rostrocaudal axis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F) or between Mo and SS (Figure 2G, H), but exhibits increased density toward deeper layers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2G, H.

claim: dOLs and LCOLs exhibit increased density toward deeper layers.
source: In contrast, the distribution of dOLs and LCOLs do not vary significantly across the rostrocaudal axis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F) or between Mo and SS (Figure 2G, H), but exhibits increased density toward deeper layers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Cortical MPOLs have been observed in mice as old as 1 year.
source: Importantly, we have observed cortical MPOLs in mice as old as 1 year (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H), well beyond the age analyzed in previous reports (Kessaris et al., 2006; Orduz et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021), suggesting a persisted contribution.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2H.

claim: The observation of cortical MPOLs in 1-year-old mice is well beyond the age analyzed in previous reports.
source: Importantly, we have observed cortical MPOLs in mice as old as 1 year (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H), well beyond the age analyzed in previous reports (Kessaris et al., 2006; Orduz et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021), suggesting a persisted contribution.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited literature.

claim: The observation of cortical MPOLs in 1-year-old mice suggests a persisted contribution.
source: Importantly, we have observed cortical MPOLs in mice as old as 1 year (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H), well beyond the age analyzed in previous reports (Kessaris et al., 2006; Orduz et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021), suggesting a persisted contribution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of MPOLs in 1-year-old mice.

claim: Piriform cortex contains higher proportions of LCOLs than dOLs.
source: Different from the neocortex, Pir contains higher proportions (Figure 2J) of LCOLs than dOLs.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: MPOLs make the lowest contribution to piriform cortex.
source: MPOLs make the lowest contribution (Figure 2J) at a density similar to SS and higher than Mo (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2J and Figure 2I.

claim: MPOLs in piriform cortex have a density similar to SS and higher than Mo.
source: MPOLs make the lowest contribution (Figure 2J) at a density similar to SS and higher than Mo (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Corpus callosum is mainly populated by dOLs and supplemented by very low proportions of LCOLs and MPOLs.
source: We found that, similar to the neocortex, cc is mainly populated by dOLs and supplemented by very low proportions of LCOLs and MPOLs (Figure 2K–N).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2K–N.

claim: LCOLs and MPOLs show preferential distribution in the lateral and medial regions of corpus callosum (cc-l and cc-m), respectively.
source: Interestingly, LCOLs and MPOLs seem to show preferential distribution in the lateral and medial regions of cc (cc-l and cc-m), respectively (Figure 2L–N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2L–N.

claim: Anterior commissure is mainly populated by LCOLs and MPOLs and supplemented by very low proportion of dOLs.
source: Different from cc, ac is mainly populated by LCOLs and MPOLs and supplemented by very low proportion of dOLs (Figure 2K–N).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2K–N.

claim: All RFP+ cells are ASPA+, reassuring the specificity of the labeling strategies.
source: Notably, all RFP+ cells are ASPA+, reassured the specificity of our label strategies.
evidence: This is supported by co-staining data.

claim: RFP−ASPA+ cells were difficult to find in Mo, SS, and cc, but were more easily observed in Pir and ac, consistent with the respective low and high LCOL contributions in these regions.
source: RFP−ASPA+ cells were difficult to find in Mo, SS, and cc, but were more easily observed in Pir and ac, consistent with the respective low and high LCOL contributions in these regions.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The lack of LCOL in neocortex is less likely caused by competitive postnatal elimination, but more likely due to limited production and/or allocation.
source: The lack of adult labeling in our study together with the lack of developmental labeling in the other study suggests that the lack of LCOL in neocortex is less likely caused by competitive postnatal elimination, but more likely due to limited production and/or allocation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: In utero electroporation failed to label LGE-derived cortical OLs in both embryonic and early postnatal brains.
source: This finding is supported by another report in which in utero electroporation failed to label LGE-derived cortical OLs in both embryonic and early postnatal brains, and an exclusion strategy revealed very low percentage of LGE/CGE-derived cortical OLs in neonatal brains (Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2023.

claim: An exclusion strategy revealed very low percentage of LGE/CGE-derived cortical OLs in neonatal brains.
source: This finding is supported by another report in which in utero electroporation failed to label LGE-derived cortical OLs in both embryonic and early postnatal brains, and an exclusion strategy revealed very low percentage of LGE/CGE-derived cortical OLs in neonatal brains (Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2023.

claim: The corpus callosum showed a similar OL composition as the neocortex.
source: In addition, we found that the cc showed a similar OL composition as the neocortex, but the Pir and the ac each exhibited distinct OL compositions in term of their embryonic origins.
evidence: This is a finding based on the quantitative data presented.

claim: The piriform cortex and the anterior commissure each exhibited distinct OL compositions in terms of their embryonic origins.
source: In addition, we found that the cc showed a similar OL composition as the neocortex, but the Pir and the ac each exhibited distinct OL compositions in term of their embryonic origins.
evidence: This is a finding based on the quantitative data presented.

claim: LCOLs are the major contributor to both piriform cortex and anterior commissure.
source: LCOLs are the major contributor to both regions, while dOLs and MPOLs mainly contribute to Pir and ac, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2.

claim: dOLs mainly contribute to piriform cortex.
source: LCOLs are the major contributor to both regions, while dOLs and MPOLs mainly contribute to Pir and ac, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2.

claim: MPOLs mainly contribute to anterior commissure.
source: LCOLs are the major contributor to both regions, while dOLs and MPOLs mainly contribute to Pir and ac, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The OpalinP2A-Flpo-T2A-tTA2 allele was generated by targeted insertion of the T2A-Flpo-P2A-tTA2 sequence immediately before the STOP codon of the endogenous Opalin gene using homologous recombination.
source: The OpalinP2A-Flpo-T2A-tTA2 allele was generated by targeted insertion of the T2A-Flpo-P2A-tTA2 sequence immediately before the STOP codon of the endogenous Opalin gene using homologous recombination.
evidence: This is a description of the method used to generate the new driver.

claim: Flpo and tTA2 were inserted before the STOP codon and linked by self-cleavage peptide P2A and T2A, allowing co-transcription and translation with Opalin.
source: In OpalinP2A-Flpo-T2A-tTA2, Flpo and tTA2 were inserted before the STOP codon and linked by self-cleavage peptide P2A and T2A (Figure 1A–C), allowing co-transcription and translation with Opalin.
evidence: This is a description of the design of the new driver shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: The intersectional strategy combining OpalinFlp and ProgenitorCre with Ai65 labels OLs derived from Cre+ progenitor domain by RFP.
source: (1) combining OpalinFlp and ProgenitorCre with intersectional reporters Ai65 to label OLs derived from Cre+ progenitor domain by RFP (Figure 2A);
evidence: This is a description of the genetic strategy shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The subtractional strategy combining OpalinFlp and ProgenitorCre with RC::FLTG simultaneously labels OLs derived from Cre+ progenitors by GFP and OLs derived from the complementing Cre− progenitors by RFP.
source: (2) combining OpalinFlp and ProgenitorCre with RC::FLTG (Plummer et al., 2015) to simultaneously label OLs derived from Cre+ progenitors by green fluorescent protein (GFP) and OLs derived from the complementing Cre− progenitors by RFP (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the genetic strategy shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The subtraction power of the combinatorial strategy enabled targeting of OLs derived from LGE/CGE progenitors that express neither Emx1 nor Nkx2.1.
source: Importantly, the subtraction power enabled us to target OLs derived from LGE/CGE progenitors that express neither Emx1 nor Nkx2.1 (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a description of the capability of the genetic strategy shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The combinatorial strategies greatly facilitated the identification of OLs derived from specific origin which exist at relatively low density in certain regions.
source: In addition, these strategies greatly facilitated the identification of OLs derived from specific origin which exist at relatively low density in certain regions.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the genetic strategies.
